name: OPA810IDBVR
title: 140 MHz FET-input op amp with rail-to-rail inputs and output
summary: OPA810 is a single FET-input voltage-feedback op amp, stable at unity gain, with 140 MHz small-signal bandwidth, 70 MHz GBWP and 200 V/µs slew rate on 3.7 mA. Input bias current is 2 pA typical and inputs and output reach both rails; a JFET main stage hands over to a CMOS auxiliary stage near the positive rail. It runs from 4.75 V to 27 V, drives 75 mA linearly, takes 7 V between its inputs, and is specified from -40°C to +125°C in SOIC-8, SOT-23-5 and SC70-5.
key_figures: 4.75 V to 27 V total (±2.375 V to ±13.5 V)
100 µV typ; 500 µV max SOIC, 715 µV max DBV and DCK (10 V)

circuits.title: Noninverting amplifier
circuits.description: The signal enters the noninverting input; RG returns the inverting input to the reference VREF and RF closes the loop from the output. Gain is 1 + RF/RG and the output sits at VREF with no signal. VREF is usually mid-supply on a single supply and often ground on split supplies.
notes: VIN is the signal VSIG riding on VREF; the output is (1 + RF/RG) × VSIG about VREF.

circuits.title: Inverting amplifier
circuits.description: The noninverting input is held at VREF. The signal drives the inverting input through RG and RF feeds back from the output, so the gain is -RF/RG about VREF.
notes: VIN is the signal VSIG riding on VREF; the output is -(RF/RG) × VSIG about VREF.

circuits.title: Unity-gain buffer driving a capacitive load through RS
circuits.description: A follower whose output reaches the load capacitance CL and the resistive load RL through a series resistor RS. RS adds a zero that cancels the pole CL forms with the amplifier's output impedance, keeping the loop stable. Up to 10 pF needs no RS; larger loads at unity gain use the RS values of Figure 6-3.

parts.note: 56 Ω at 22 pF, 40 Ω at 33 pF, 47 Ω at 47 pF in Figure 6-3

circuits.title: Noninverting gain of 5 V/V, noise comparison
circuits.description: A gain-of-5 noninverting stage on ±5 V with a source resistance RS from the noninverting input to ground. Case 1 uses RS = 200 Ω, RG = 250 Ω, RF = 1 kΩ and gives 34 nV/√Hz at the output; case 2 scales every resistor by ten and gives 51.5 nV/√Hz, the resistor noise then rivalling the amplifier's own.

circuits.title: Wideband 100 kΩ transimpedance amplifier
circuits.description: A reverse-biased photodiode feeds the inverting input; RF = 100 kΩ converts its current to voltage, and the total feedback capacitance of 1.03 pF (CF plus board parasitics) sets a maximally flat response for a 20 pF diode. The noninverting input is grounded, supplies are ±5 V, and the output drives an oscilloscope's 50 Ω input through a series resistor. Estimated bandwidth is 2.19 MHz; simulation gives 3 MHz with 62° phase margin.

parts.note: series output resistor into the 50 Ω scope input

circuits.title: High-impedance data-acquisition front end
circuits.description: Two OPA810 followers on ±12 V present a picoamp-bias, high-impedance input to each side of a differential signal, each behind an RC filter. A THS4561 fully differential amplifier on 12 V and -0.2 V scales the pair through RG and RF (with CF) to the ADS9110 18-bit, 2 MSPS converter, through RS and CCB at each ADC input; its output common mode comes from the REF5050 5.0 V reference. The ADC reference input is driven by an OPA378 and OPA837 in a composite loop from the filtered REF5050 output.

parts.note: in series with C3 across the FDA inputs

circuits.title: Unity-gain buffer after a multiplexer
circuits.description: Several high-impedance sensors share one signal chain: a multiplexer selects a channel and one OPA810 follower drives the ADC. Each channel switch steps the buffer input, so settling and the allowed differential input voltage matter; the built-in input clamps take up to 7 V between the inputs during the slew without series resistors (Figure 8-18).

operation.text: Single voltage-feedback op amp with a FET input, stable at unity gain. Runs from 4.75 V to 27 V total, 140 MHz small-signal bandwidth at unity gain, 70 MHz GBWP, 200 V/µs slew rate, 6.3 nV/√Hz voltage noise and 3.7 mA quiescent current. Input bias current stays in the picoamp range across the whole common-mode range. Built on a SiGe BiCMOS process. A dual version is sold as OPA2810.

The main input is a JFET differential pair; an auxiliary CMOS pair takes over within 2.5 V of the positive supply. Together they give rail-to-rail input with no phase reversal and bias current no higher than 20 pA anywhere in the common-mode range. With the input in the auxiliary stage CMRR and PSRR are 75 dB typical. Lowest offset, noise and distortion come with the common mode more than 2.5 V below VS+.

Internal clamps allow up to 7 V between the inputs (or the total supply, whichever is lower), against one or two diode drops for a usual op amp. Input bias current is limited to about 300 µA when clamped (Figure 6-54), so the source is not loaded and no current-limiting resistors are needed while the inputs stay within the supplies. This suits multiplexed inputs, fast transients, and use as a comparator for fault detection.

The output swings rail to rail (Figure 6-15 at 10 V). After saturation it recovers in 55 ns with the inputs 0.5 V past the supplies at G = -1 V/V on 10 V. The output is short-circuit protected (Figure 6-16). It delivers 75 mA of linear output current and can source and sink heavy currents without loss of linearity.

Up to 10 pF can be driven directly. Larger loads at unity gain need a series resistor between output and load (Figure 6-3); at gains above 1 V/V more than 10 pF can be driven without one (Figure 6-4).

Every pin has ESD diodes to both supplies; they carry about 10 mA continuous. The differential clamps limit bias current only while the common mode is inside the supplies. If the inputs can go beyond the supplies, add series input resistors, kept as small as possible because they add noise and cut bandwidth.

Split supplies from ±2.375 V to ±13.5 V put mid-supply at ground, convenient for ground-referenced signals and lab equipment; VREF then goes to ground. A single supply of 4.75 V to 27 V with VS- at ground works with no loss of performance if input and output stay in the linear range; shift all levels by half the supply. A grounded low rail also removes the -PSRR error. Unbalanced bipolar supplies work too.

RF and RG trade stability, feedback-network power and noise. Large values save output power but add voltage and current noise and, with the inverting-node capacitance, put a pole in the feedback factor that cuts phase margin, causing peaking and lower bandwidth (Figures 8-6 to 8-8). Small values cost power and load the output, raising distortion. A 2 kΩ resistor has 5.75 nV/√Hz thermal noise, close to the amplifier's flat-band noise, so RF under 2 kΩ keeps resistor noise below the amplifier's own.

Key inputs are the diode capacitance at its bias, the gain RF and the 70 MHz GBWP. In the 100 kΩ, 20 pF example the 1/β curve has a zero at 70 kHz from RF and CIN and a pole at 1.5 MHz from RF and CF, crossing AOL at 20 dB per decade; simulated phase margin is 62° and bandwidth 3 MHz.

With an 8 V step at a follower's input the amplifier slews and its inputs part by up to 7 V until the output arrives (Figure 8-18). The clamps take this with no series resistors, no damage and no shift in specifications; parts rated for 0.7 V to 1.5 V would need series resistors that also cut bandwidth.

Place 0.01 µF high-frequency capacitors within 0.1 in of the supply pins, with a larger capacitor (2.2 µF typical, 2.2 µF to 6.8 µF in the layout guidance) on each supply that can sit farther away and be shared by nearby devices. Single supply: on VS+ only; split supply: from each rail to ground. A capacitor across the two rails on split supplies lowers second-harmonic distortion. AC performance is slightly better at 10 V, with little more supply current.

Keep parasitic capacitance off the signal pins: open ground and power planes under the inverting input and output on all layers, with planes unbroken elsewhere. Capacitance at the output and inverting input can cause instability; at the noninverting input it band-limits with the source impedance. Use short, wide supply traces to the decoupling capacitors. Use surface-mount or low-reactance resistors, never wirewound; place RF and any output series resistor right at the output pin, and RG close to the inverting input. Resistors have about 0.2 pF shunt capacitance, which above 10 kΩ puts a pole or zero near the 70 MHz GBWP. Do not socket the part.

A short trace and the next input form a lumped capacitive load: use wide traces (50 mils to 100 mils), open the planes under them, and pick RS for phase margin. Loads under 10 pF need no RS since the part is compensated for a 10 pF parasitic load; higher gain allows more. Long runs can be matched transmission lines, series-matched at the source and shunt-terminated at the destination with a 6 dB loss, or series-terminated only. A 50 Ω environment is not needed on board; a higher impedance gives lower distortion.

No heat sink or airflow is needed in most uses. Quiescent power equals the unloaded supply current multiplied by the full supply voltage. At 125°C ambient in SOIC (134.8°C/W), 24 V × 4.7 mA gives 113 mW and a 15°C rise before load power is added.
